headline: Sixteen documented examples called APIs that do not exist — `b.db.from(t).insert()`, `b.scheduler.every()`, `b.httpClient.create()`, `b.https.createServer()` and more, each throwing on the first line an operator copied
summary:
The gate that executes `@example` blocks could only run the self-contained ones. Anything opening a database, starting a listener, writing a file or generating a key was skipped — about 600 examples, and "skipped" was doing a lot of quiet work, because a renamed method inside any of them is exactly the drift the gate exists to catch.

Those now execute too, each batch in its own process, under Node's permission model, with its own database and working directory. The first run found 32 failures. Sixteen were real: examples teaching methods the framework does not have. `b.db.from("orders").insert({…})` appeared five times — the API is `insertOne`. `b.https.createServer` appeared three times — there is no `b.https`; the operator uses Node's own. `b.db.handle()` appeared five times across the crypto-field, DSR, IMAP and JMAP docs — `b.db` IS the handle.

All sixteen are corrected. The gate now executes about 990 examples instead of 676 — the exact number moves with what the machine allows, since an example that reaches the network counts differently offline.

Some of what it still skips is now DECLARED rather than guessed at: an example that needs an operator's running app, a writable path, an OS keychain or outbound network says so in a `// requires:` line that renders on its own documentation page, where the reader sees the prerequisite too. The rest is still inferred from what the example throws — an identifier only the surrounding prose defines, a module the framework does not ship, a precondition the framework itself refuses — and that inference is invisible to the reader. Those are the ones left to declare.

items.title: Sixteen examples documented methods that do not exist
items.body:
Each of these throws immediately for anyone who copies it:

- `b.db.from(t).insert({…})` — five examples, across `from`, `transaction`, `hashFor`, `exportCsv` and `eraseHard`. The query builder has `insertOne` and `insertMany`.
- `b.https.createServer(…)` — three examples in the TLS-exporter docs. There is no `b.https`; those examples now require Node's `node:https`, which is what they always meant.
- `b.db.handle()` — five examples, in the crypto-field, DSR, IMAP and JMAP docs. `b.db` is itself the handle those APIs want.
- `b.scheduler.every(ms, fn)` — the scheduler is `create()` then `register(name, ms, fn)` then `start()`.
- `b.httpClient.create({ baseUrl })` — the pinned client is `pinnedClient(client, allowedHosts)`, wrapping a request-capable client.
- `b.network.tls.reload()`, `b.externalDb.backend(name)`, `b.objectStore.put(key, body)`, `b.worker.create(…)` — none exist. The cluster example also documented `externalDbBackend` as an object when it takes the NAME of a backend registered through `externalDb.init`, so the option list was wrong alongside the example.
- `gate.decide(…)` on a guard gate — the method is `check(…)`.
- `b.openapi.security.bearer({ bearerFormat })` and `b.mail.create({ host, port })` — both named options the validators reject; the log-stream local sink example passed `path` where the sink requires `dir`.
- Two ACME examples used `crypto.generateKeyPairSync` without requiring `node:crypto`, which resolves to the WebCrypto global and has no such method.
- One JOSE example read `pair.mlkem.publicKey` from a key pair whose shape is `{ publicKey, privateKey, ecPublicKey, ecPrivateKey }`.

A second check reads every `b.…` path an example NAMES and resolves it against the shipped surface. Execution stops at the first throw, so a placeholder the surrounding prose defines ends an example before anything after it is reached — which is where `b.db.handle()` was still sitting in the POP3 and ManageSieve docs, and where `b.C.BYTES.gib()`, `b.C.TIME.days()` (the namespace is `b.constants`), `b.journal.append()`, `b.network.tls.context()` and `b.db.raw()` were hiding. Seven more corrections, none of which running the examples could have found.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` 0.4.14 → 0.4.15
items.body: The PKI toolkit behind `b.mtlsCa` gains real answers for two revocation shapes it previously reported as undetermined: a CA that partitions revocations by reason code, and one that publishes a delta CRL alongside its base.

items.title: An HTTP/2 test server outlived the test that started it
items.body: `Http2Server.close()` stops accepting and then waits for live sessions, so a server closed while its peer session was still tearing down stayed listening after its test had finished — and the three call sites in the HTTP-client suite did not await it at all. Under a parallel run that surfaced as the end-of-run handle check reporting a listener nobody owned, which is the flake the shared drain was built to make attributable. It named the socket and its port; the servers now end their sessions and wait for the close.

items.title: An abort test measured the runner instead of the abort
items.body: The assertion that aborting a five-second `safeAsync.sleep` short-circuits it required the call to return within 200ms. That is a measure of how promptly a loaded machine delivers a 20ms timer, not of whether the abort worked, and it failed under a parallel run. The bound is now well below the sleep it cancels: nothing but a working abort can return early, and scheduler jitter cannot fail it.

items.title: An example may declare the environment it assumes
items.body:
Some examples describe a call against an application that is already running — a configured views directory, a registered database backend, a tracer, a signing passphrase. They cannot execute in a test process and pretending otherwise would only produce noise.

Such an example now says so on its first line: `// requires: a views directory on disk`. The gate skips it, and the line renders on the primitive's own page, so an operator reading the documentation learns the prerequisite at the same time. This is deliberately a marker in the documentation rather than a skip list inside the test — a list would cost nothing to add and tell a reader nothing.

items.title: every documented example is executed, not just the safe ones
items.body:
The examples that touch real resources now run in child processes, in batches, each with its own database and working directory, a per-example ceiling and a watchdog on the batch. A batch that is killed reports everything it completed and names the example it stopped at, so a wedge is attributable rather than a silent gap.

They run under Node's permission model, because a disposable working directory is not containment: these are the examples selected for spawning processes, writing files and calling out, and several name absolute paths like `/var/log/app.log` and `/opt/app/app.bin`. Changing the working directory only redirects the relative ones. Writes are confined to the run's own tree and the OS temp directory; starting a subprocess is denied outright. Turning it on immediately caught ten examples that had been attempting real host paths, each of which now declares what it needs.

Three more things had to be right for the results to mean anything. Results go to a file rather than stdout, because the examples boot framework machinery that logs JSON there and those lines are indistinguishable from result records. An example runs in the child's own realm rather than a sandbox realm, or a `RegExp` literal it passes to the framework fails every `instanceof` check on the way in and a perfectly good example reads as broken. And the database is rebuilt per example rather than per batch — it is a process singleton, so one example that re-opens it under a different posture leaves the next failing for reasons of its own; when process-global state cannot be undone that way, the child hands its remaining work to a fresh process rather than guess.

A throw from a callback the example scheduled counts against that example, and running past the ceiling in a child is a failure rather than a skip: those are the wedged and the late-failing examples this pass exists to reach.

Coverage went from 676 executed to about 990, the remainder varying with what the machine running it allows.
